Brazil’s President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's election win has triggered financial uncertainty as right-wing candidate Flavio Bolsonaro has refused to concede [Juan Barreto/AFP]By Al Jazeera Staff and ReutersPublished On 26 Oct 202626 Oct 2026
Brazil’s real dropped against the United States dollar on the heels of Brazil’s President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s unexpected re-election after right-wing Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, led in the first round of voting earlier this month.
Brazil’s currency dropped against the dollar by 12 percent in spot trading. Bovespa stock index futures tumbled nearly 15 percent on Monday.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3World reacts to Lula’s victory in Brazil’s presidential electionlist 2 of 3Lula’s victory may be a turning point for Latin Americalist 3 of 3How did Lula beat Bolsonaro after losing Brazil’s first-round election?end of list
“I’m not surprised the real is sinking sharply; traders are covering their bets that assume a Bolsonaro victory and tighter fiscal policy,” Rachel Ziemba, adjunct senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security, told Al Jazeera.
Brazil’s stock exchange halted trading for 30 minutes. The Bovespa index fell 10 percent from its previous close, triggering a circuit-breaker safety mechanism and reversing a rally earlier this month amid expectations of a shift to the right after Bolsonaro won the first round.
Ziemba says Bolsonaro’s refusal to concede the election has driven some financial uncertainty.
“The market pressure is also amplified by the objections raised by Bolsonaro, but the scale of the victory suggests that the result will stand,” she said.

By Alia Chughtai and Hoda SherifPublished On 26 Oct 202626 Oct 2026
On November 3, about 210 million registered voters will decide how much power Donald Trump has for the rest of his US presidency.
Trump is not on the ballot, but control of the United States Congress is. Made up of the House of Representatives and the Senate, Congress writes the country’s laws and controls federal spending.
Recommended Stories list of 4 itemslist 1 of 4Obama slams Trump’s ‘cruelty and corruption’ as he rallies Democratslist 2 of 4Election posters, mass tourism and property: Israel’s footprint in Cypruslist 3 of 4‘Unnecessary’ Iran war, corruption: Takeaways from Obama’s midterm speecheslist 4 of 4CENTCOM reportedly has plans for Iran strikes: Will Trump approve them?end of list
In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera breaks down how the elections work, which races matter and what the results could mean for either party.
What happens in the midterm elections?
Held halfway through a US president’s four-year term, midterm elections decide the makeup of Congress.
All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 of the Senate’s 100 seats are being contested, including special elections in the states of Florida and Ohio to fill the seats vacated by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vice President JD Vance. Voters in 36 states will also elect governors.
House members represent one congressional district each and serve two-year terms, while senators serve six-year terms.
Midterm elections are also widely considered a referendum on the sitting president’s performance.
Since 1946, the president’s party has lost an average of 26.5 seats in the House and a handful in the Senate in midterm elections, according to Todd Belt, a professor of political management at George Washington University. ...

item.title: How Venezuela’s earthquake amputees adapt to life without limbs
item.description:
How Venezuela’s earthquake amputees adapt to life without limbs
Experts say recovery for earthquake survivors will likely be a lifelong endeavour, given the physical and mental toll of the June 24 tragedy.A line of prosthetic limbs on display in the Ortoprotecnica clinic in Caracas, Venezuela [Catherine Ellis/Al Jazeera]A line of prosthetic limbs on display in the Ortoprotecnica clinic in Caracas, Venezuela [Catherine Ellis/Al Jazeera]By Catherine EllisPublished On 26 Oct 202626 Oct 2026

Ricardo Contreras’s new leg rests on a wooden countertop.
More than four months after twin earthquakes struck Venezuela, the 24-year-old is still recovering from his injuries.
When he was trapped beneath the rubble on the night of June 24, he waited hours to be rescued. His left leg had been pinned beneath a fallen door frame, limiting its blood circulation. It had to be amputated.
“One of the biggest achievements is that we survived,” Ricardo said, glancing towards his 16-year-old brother, Andres Contreras. “At first, when I found out Andres was well, I didn’t care about my leg too much. I would have chosen a thousand times over for Andres to be OK.”
But now Ricardo is adapting to his new reality.
He and his brother are still undergoing physiotherapy for their injuries. On a scorching afternoon, he sits in a small workshop in the hills of northwestern Caracas, waiting to do rehabilitation exercises to prepare for his new prosthetic leg.
“Now it’s about regaining a little of the independence I had before the earthquake, because that’s what limits me most," Ricardo said.
But recovery is only part of the challenge he is facing. His parents died in the collapse.
Resources and aid have also grown scarcer, particularly as global attention faded and international donations dried up.

Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune [File: Nadja Wohlleben/Reuters]By Al Jazeera Staff and ReutersPublished On 26 Oct 202626 Oct 2026
Algeria’s President Abdelmadjid Tebboune has ordered troops to neighbouring Niger to protect energy and economic interests shared by both countries.
The decision, announced by Algeria’s presidency on Monday, came after both chambers of parliament approved the deployment in an emergency session on Sunday.
Recommended Stories list of 2 itemslist 1 of 2Algeria’s military deployment to Niger: What’s behind the move?list 2 of 2Algerian parliament’s upper house approves troop deployment to Nigerend of list
The presidency said authorities in Niger had requested military assistance.
If carried out, it would be Algeria’s first overseas military deployment since 1973, when it sent soldiers to support Egypt during the Arab-Israeli war.
The move marks a departure from Algeria’s longstanding reluctance to intervene militarily beyond its borders.
A 2020 constitutional reform allows the president to authorise overseas deployments with the approval of at least two-thirds of legislators in each parliamentary chamber.
Algeria sent fighter jets and support aircraft to Niger in August after what Algerian officials described as an attempt to destabilise its military government.
The presidency said the deployment decision was made under provisions of Algeria’s constitution allowing the military to operate abroad with parliamentary approval.
It has not been announced how many soldiers will be sent or when.
Algerian Senator Belkacem Boulghiti told reporters after Sunday’s parliamentary vote that the soldiers would protect economic infrastructure, particularly Algerian oil facilities in Niger.

The United Kingdom has sanctioned 15 Sudanese military commanders, militia leaders and security officials from both sides of the ongoing civil war accused of committing war crimes during the fall of the city of el-Fasher.
Commanders from the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces were sanctioned for sexual violence, torture and attacks on civilians. The measures include travel bans and asset freezes, with the wider aim of ensuring that “the horrors that took place at El Fasher will be known to the world”, the UK Foreign Office said.

The announcement came after the release of UK-funded reporting by the Centre for Information Resilience, which revealed a campaign of “systematic starvation and conflict-related sexual violence against civilians in Sudan”, the Foreign Office added.
On Monday, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said those who perpetrated crimes against humanity “must be held accountable and support from all external backers to the warring parties must end”.
The move comes one year after the fall of the city of el-Fasher, which became a focal point of Sudan’s war last year as civilians faced a prolonged siege, reported mass killings, widespread sexual violence and attacks on hospitals.

The UN says that Russia's persistent attacks on Ukrainian civilian targets and the weaponisation of winter cold constitute war crimes (File: AP)By ReutersPublished On 26 Oct 202626 Oct 2026
Russia’s persistent attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure constitute war crimes as they weaponise the cold of winter, a United Nations commission has said.
The Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine laid out in a report submitted to the UN General Assembly on Monday years of Russian attacks on heating plants, power lines, gas facilities and other infrastructure since the autumn of 2022.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Europe needs a war economylist 2 of 3Russia drops cluster bombs on Ukraine as Kyiv consolidates front linelist 3 of 3Aleksandar Vucic, the Serbian leader brought down by studentsend of list
The report was issued as Russia has stepped up its attacks on such civilian targets. Moscow has sought every year since its full-scale invasion in February 2022 to inflict suffering on Ukrainian citizens with an apparent ambition of draining the country’s will and ability to continue to defend its territory.
The commission said it has investigated the impact on civilians of large-scale attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and their cumulative effect since 2022.
“The frequency, intensity and geographic range of systematic waves of attacks with hundreds of drones and missiles at a time have increased over the years and inflicted significant damage to Ukraine’s energy sector,” the report noted.
